Negative Appraisals.value: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
I feel like I don't know myself anymore
I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me

vignette: Soraya was thirty-nine when the coordinated bombing at the central transit hub shattered the ordinary rhythm of her life. She had been waiting on the platform when the concussive blast threw her against a tiled pillar, followed by the sharp, unpredictable cracks of gunfire echoing through the station’s vaulted ceilings. In the sudden smoke, armed officers pushed through the crowd, their shouted commands and raised weapons indistinguishable from the attackers she had just witnessed. The terror was not just in the violence itself, but in the rapid convergence of uniformed responders and the deafening whir of rescue helicopters cutting through the smoke-choked sky. When she returned to her role as a project manager overseeing municipal infrastructure, the world had quietly shifted. The downtown corridor outside her glass-walled conference room became a landscape of potential danger. Whenever a marked police cruiser slowed past the building lobby, Soraya would feel the familiar alarm ring out, her thoughts instantly pulling her back to the plaza where she had watched lifeless bodies sprawl across the pavement. She began to steer her route away from the construction site she visited weekly, bracing herself whenever she caught the distant drone of aircraft overhead, and would abruptly lose her train of thought whenever a colleague raised their voice in frustration, her attention locking onto the sudden volume as a signal of imminent violence. The boardroom, once a space for strategy and collaboration, now felt like an interrogation chamber where every loud noise or uniformed delivery driver at the service entrance confirmed her worst fears. The moment these familiar alarms flared inside her, they did not simply fade. Instead, the sight of uniformed officers or the sharp report of a backfiring car seemed to rewrite her understanding of who she had become. She would sit in her office and realize she no longer recognized the woman in the mirror; the laughter she used to bring to family dinners had vanished, replaced by a heavy, unyielding misery that made every day feel like a weight she could not set down. Even a fleeting glance from a colleague across a crowded breakroom triggered a cold realization, convincing her that whatever had fractured inside her was visible to everyone, that her trauma was written across her face like a permanent mark no one could ignore. The triggers did not just signal danger; they actively dismantled her self-concept, transforming routine moments into proof of her own brokenness. Each encounter with authority or sudden violence acted as a catalyst, pushing her past mere fear and into a deep, personal conviction that she was fundamentally damaged and unmistakably exposed. Over the months, this reflexive spiral became a habit she could no longer outpace. She started declining site visits to avoid the street-level chaos, delegating her presentations to avoid the scrutiny she felt in boardrooms, and eventually stopped attending neighborhood gatherings where police patrols or loud engines might pass by. Her marriage, once sustained by shared weekends and easy conversation, grew strained as she withdrew into a rigid routine, leaving her husband to wonder why the woman he married had become a stranger who flinched at her own reflection. The distance was not born of anger, but of a quiet conviction that she had become unrecognizable to everyone who still knew her. The breaking point arrived not with a single event, but with the quiet realization that her withdrawal was collapsing the very stability she worked so hard to build. She finally sat in a therapist’s office not because she wanted to relive the blast, but because she needed a way to stop the dread that hijacked her mornings and because she was exhausted by the fear that everyone around her could see the damage she believed was permanent. What she hoped for was simply a return to the person she used to be, a way to quiet the alarms before they stole her happiness and erased her identity again.
